27.t: First D.C. job with Johnny Ridgely's small band
27.s: Dan Andrews, who went to Howard, had urged him to come; within a week Phillips was in Johnny Ridgely's five or six piece band, living on Corcoran Street.
27.q: Oh, when I first got here, I didn't know nobody but Dan -- Dan Andrews. See, when the band broke up, he came here. He didn't go nowhere.

27.t: Leaving Tommy Miles's band for Long Branch, 1941
27.s: Phillips left the Miles band in late May or June 1941 to go to Long Branch, New Jersey.
27.q: Must have been about... I left then and I went to Long Branch, New Jersey. It must have been round about June -- the latter part of May or the first of June.

27.t: Working at a hotel in Long Branch and living in Asbury Park, summer 1941
27.s: The band played 8 to 12 at the Scarbourn Hotel; Phillips and Tex Briscoe lived in lively Asbury Park for 35 dollars more and commuted by train until Labor Day.
27.ch: Long Branch and the war years
27.q: Well, we went up there, took six pieces up there, and stayed on this job. Had a helluva good job. Paid good money, and we went to work at 8 and got off at 12. We'd go around to all the beaches and all the clubs, and stay up til 5-6 o'clock in the morning, all around Asbury Park. That's where we…

27.t: The 1942 walk-a-thon bands at Turner's Arena and 26th Street
27.s: Back in D.C., Phillips played Tex Briscoe's eight-piece band for a summer-long walk-a-thon with Fats Wright, Osie Johnson and John Malachi, moving to a second one on 26th Street until November 1942.
27.ch: Long Branch and the war years
27.q: : After I came back from Asbury Park, they had a walk-a-thon here. Up there at Turner's Arena. I don't know if you remember that or not. That's between 14th and 13th on W Street. That was a big place where all the bands used to come, good shows -- big arena. They had a walk-a-thon there for the…

27.t: John Malachi's band at Dykes Stockade and Crystal Caverns, 1943
27.s: Malachi took six players to Dykes, which closed with gas rationing; Benny Carwell then hired the band at Crystal Caverns on Willie Bryant's recommendation, with Charlie Rouse, Osie Johnson and Tommy Potter, from February 1943.
27.ch: Long Branch and the war years
27.q: Yeah. He got one out in Dykes Stockade. When that one was over, John got this job at the Dykes, and then he took six pieces out there. He took me, he took Cragbrains and Curtis, and Tommy Potter on bass...

27.t: Malachi's players leave for Trummy Young and Phillips takes over the band
27.s: Malachi, Harry Curtis and Tommy Potter went with Trummy Young and Osie Johnson went into the service, so Phillips led the Crystal Caverns band until August 1944.
27.ch: Long Branch and the war years
27.q: John and them left and went with Trummy. It must have been... It was in the Fall of the year. No, it wasn't... Was it in the Fall? Because I stayed there about a year, and then I quit. Yeah, it was in the Fall.

27.t: Playing with Coridge Davis at Club Bali and in Atlantic City
27.s: From late 1944 Phillips played with Coridge Davis at Club Bali on 14th and T in Washington and from June 1945 in Atlantic City.
27.q: In '44 I played a club that I went into with him... Around the latter part of the year, I played at Club Bali at 14th and T. During the war-time that was an awfully big club. They had big shows and everything. Everybody came there. Pearl Bailey, Lena Horne. They all came in that club.

27.t: Six months at a Portsmouth club, then to Washington in 1935
27.s: Francis Whitby wrote that he had a club job in Portsmouth; Phillips, Red Elkins and others played it for six months in 1934 and he reached Washington in February 1935.
27.q: : No, no, no. See, Francis Whitby, he stayed in Portsmouth. He was sick. And he wrote a letter and told us that he knew the band wasn't doing nothing, and he had a good job for us. And he kind of wanted to come. He said he'd like to have me and Red and Sam and Charlie and Duff -- that was it.…

27.t: Going to Long Branch, New Jersey with Tommy Chase, 1941
27.s: In June 1941 Phillips joined a six-piece summer band led by pianist-trumpeter Tommy Chase, with tenor Leo Williams; Dupre and Phillips mix up Leo Williams and Leo Parker.
27.ch: Long Branch and the war years
27.q: Yeah. I went up there with Tommy Chase -- this guy around here named Chase. He's dead now. A piano player. He played piano and trumpet.

27.t: The Hanger Club with Booker Coleman, 1936
27.s: After the Ridgely club folded Phillips played about six months with Booker Coleman at the Hanger Club near the Fourteenth Street Bridge, July to winter 1936.
27.q: I stayed with him for about a year. Then the man folded the club up. The club folded up. Then after that, I went with Booker Coleman. I went up to a club around here called the Hanger Club. That's out there right across the Fourteenth Street Bridge. There used to be an airport there, years ago.

27.t: Years of gigging, then Ivory Joe Hunter and Tiny Bradshaw
27.s: Phillips gigged around D.C. from 1946, toured with Ivory Joe Hunter in 1951 and Tiny Bradshaw in 1953, both strictly rhythm-and-blues.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: Oh yeah. And he did sweet tunes, too. "I Lost My Baby and Almost Lost My Mind" -- that's the one that made him.

27.t: With Ivory Joe Hunter's show in Baltimore, the Apollo and Philadelphia's Earle
27.s: Phillips played show music for a month in 1951 as one of four extra men, with Dinah Washington and Mope and Pope on the bill, at the Howard, Apollo and the Earle's last show.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: No, I didn't get no solos much, because I played the show. See, because he had a trumpet player in there, Little Jonesy. He used to play with Basie. He played with Don Redman, too. He was a good trumpet player. He was with him when I went with Ivory. See, I didn't stay with Ivory but about a month.…

27.s: Phillips played with Bradshaw in Washington, Baltimore and the Apollo; Bradshaw sang sentimental songs, wrote Soft and Jersey Bounce and was a showman front man.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: Gone" and sentimental tunes like that, and he had a tune called "Soft" -- that was his tune. What's this other tune that he wrote? "Jersey Bounce."

27.t: Al Dunn's Music Hall house band, then a government job from 1956
27.s: Phillips recalls the 1947 house band at the Music Hall opening with Louis Armstrong, then Albert Curtis's band until he took a government job in 1956 and retired in 1971.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: Then after that, Al Dunn got a band together, and went up to the Music Hall. Stayed up there about four months. We was the house band there. We opened up with Louis Armstrong's band. Lionel Hampton stayed up there two weeks. Tony Pastor. Cootie Williams. Jimmy Lunceford...

27.t: Young D.C. players: Frank Wess, Dude Brown and John Malachi's little band
27.s: Phillips says Frank Wess came from Oklahoma to Howard and played with Coleridge Davis, and that he gave Dude Brown his first job in 1936 from Malachi's youth band.
27.q: Yeah, he came here. He went to school here. He went to Howard. His stepfather was Chiropodous(?). They moved here. Frank Wess came here from Oklahoma, and he came here and he was... He played around here. Then he first got a good start playing with the band I was with, Coleridge Davis. They'd go up…

27.t: Osie Johnson, Claude Hopkins and other D.C. names
27.s: Phillips says Osie Johnson was 17 when he played with them in 1943, did not know Claude Hopkins's relatives, and mentions pianist Dick Hopkins.
27.q: : There's a guy named Dick Hopkins, but he's not related to... He's a piano player. Dick is a little short, fat guy. He plays a whole lot of piano. He works down at Market End.

27.t: Garnett Clark and meeting young John Malachi
27.s: Phillips barely knew Garnett Clark; he met John Malachi in 1936, a 16-year-old playing small gigs, and later played with him in Tommy Miles's band.
27.q: I didn't know him too well. He was about getting ready to leave. I think he was in New York when I came here, but he used to come down here.

27.t: House band at the Howard Theatre, 1951-54
27.s: The Howard house band directed by Frank Wess included the Pogue brothers and Buck Hill, a Dunbar student then who, like others, admired Prez.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: Oh yeah. Let's see. Frank Wess was directing the band. We had Julius Pogue, Pete Pogue, Fathead Pogue -- they was brothers; all of them played saxophone. And they had Wallace Cryer playing baritone. Buck Hill...

0.t: Bardu Ali's band at the Club Paradise, Atlantic City, and Philadelphia
0.s: Bardu Ali fronted an eleven or twelve piece band for the Club Paradise season, then took a smaller band to Philadelphia.
0.ch: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
0.q: Well, we went -- we left New York with (unintelligible) used to be the front man for Chick Webb when they were at the Savoy, and Bordu formed his own group because he had --

0.t: Charlie Gaines's band in Philadelphia and Club Harlem
0.s: After joining the Philadelphia union board Caldwell worked with Charlie Gaines in Philadelphia and at Club Harlem in Atlantic City.
0.ch: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
0.q: -- to starting? Well, I left -- when I went into the executive secretary board and (unintelligible) Philadelphia, then I started to work with Charlie Gaynes, because Charlie had one of the big, best jobs over there because that's his home, and he's worked with Leroy Smith in New York through the…

0.t: Playing in Slappy's band at Pennsauken
0.s: Slappy led a six-piece band on the river across from Camden with Ken Pope on piano and Caldwell on tenor.
0.ch: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
0.q: Oh, he had the band in Philadelphia, but he worked over in Pennsauken, New Jersey, which is just across the river, over in -- just across, outside of Camden, New Jersey, called the Radial. And he had six pieces, but it was a very fine (unintelligible) play all them big shows.

80.t: Getting the Philadelphia club job through union agent Harry Marsh
80.s: After Stuff he assembled a new group and, through drummer-union official Harry Marsh, got a job in Philadelphia that lasted two or three wartime years.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: Yeah, because I came -- I got me another group since then, and went to Philadelphia, because I heard of a job over there, through a friend of mine, drummer, and --

80.t: Leaving Fats for Stuff Smith and his own group at Philadelphia's Midway
80.s: As Fats's work was closing he left, with 'Stormy Weather' being made, and led his own group at the Midway Musical Bar in wartime Philadelphia.
80.q: Well, yes and no. I'll tell you why I said that, because I had stopped -- I had left Fats to go with well, maybe Stuff Smith. I was with Stuff for a while.

779.t: Hal playing with Tony Giardino and band members
779.s: Hal began with Giardino around 1940-41; names of drummer, bassist and trumpeter, and Hal's service dates.
779.ch: Hal, Tony Giardino and other musicians
779.q: Yeah, Charlie Cusack was playing drums with him. Remember Charlie, you met Charlie Cusack? Charlie was playing drums with him.

491.t: Tadd Dameron's Atlantic City revue at the Paradise
491.s: Dameron hired Golson and a group including Clifford Brown to play for Clarence Robinson's revue in Atlantic City.
491.ch: Reflections, marriage and early road bands
491.q: Lionel Hampton, no. Like I told you, I met Tadd with Bullmoose in ’51. Tadd hired me, because he got the gig in Atlantic City. During the summer, there was a Club Harlem. It had like a revue – chorus girls, a comedian, and a singer, this and that. Larry Steele had that group at Cafe Harlem –…

67.s: Tickets from Bobby Lee brought him and Jerry Blake to Philadelphia; Lee's band played the Cinderella Inn and Sea Girt, New Jersey.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: No, someone sent a couple of tickets to myself and Jerry Blake. Jerry Blake, he and I were -- Nashville, you know, together, we went to school together. He was in the band in Chicago with me. And we were in this thing together. And someone sent a couple of tickets to Chicago to come to…

452.t: The Zanzibar in Philadelphia and Gale Agency's Ralph Cooper
452.s: His two-week Philadelphia job packs the club, agents Ralph Cooper and Lou Leslie hear him, and Cooper pushes him over breakfast to sign with Gale Agency instead of resting.
452.ch: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
452.q: And I got away from it. And the results of this, now, let me get into it. I played in the [White] Zanzibar in Philadelphia. Gale Agency called over. Lou Leslie was the guy -- about putting in a group in the [WHITE] Zanzibar. So Dick told them, said, "Man, we got the best attraction we could have in…

75.s: He mentions joining Barnet, then recalls a summer show in Asbury Park with a drummer named Steve and Cotton Club performers, and the Rhythm Club.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: He had a band, and he used some of the Cotton Club kids, Savannah Churchill, (?)Bronson Guy(?)/found some guys(?) to do a show in Asbury Park at that time. Steve... what was his last name? He was the brother of a drummer who apparently was involved in the assassination of Jim Europe. He was a short…
